Mr. Speaker, I should like so much for us to have that opportunity-and I am sure that it will present itself, because Canada will soon have that national anthem so hoped for as well as its own national distinctive flag-for the centennial of confederation, to see all the Canadians united under the same flag in that unity which must admit diversity.
I make this appeal to all hon. members, to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) and also to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) without omitting the hon. member for Ville-neuve (Mr. Caouette). I make this appeal to the house.
Free from any prejudice, as I am myself a new member in this house, we must all strive in order that, like reasonable and intelligent people, we may give priority to reason over emotions. I repeat that like the intelligent people that we are, we ought to sit down and discuss these problems facing our beautiful country.
Mr. Speaker, this centennial of confederation, which we will celebrate soon, will be celebrated through inter-governmental exchanges such, for instance, as the one which has just occurred between the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Our celebrations will be all the more happy and satisfactory as we will encourage our youth to associate with people of either race, to mix with one another, either through associations or by frequent interprovincial visits.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is not by withdrawing-and I speak as a French speaking Quebecker-by withdrawing within the so called Quebec reserve that we will have a better future.

I prefer the words of Lord Tweedsmuir:
Give me men to match my mountains Give me men to match my plains Men with empire for a vision Men with eons in their brains.

Mr. Speaker, I love the Rockies, in the western part of my country, and I should like my friends in western Canada to feel
The Address-Mr. Prud'homme perfectly at home on Quebec's magnificent "Cap Diamant".
We have a beautiful country, one where everybody should feel at home.
We have often been asked: What do the French speaking people want? Well, I could answer that, among other things, 1 want to live while speaking French, without, on the other hand, forcing upon people who feel no need for them, my native tongue, my culture and my traditions.
May I ask my hon. friends from the prairie provinces, who perhaps do not see the need for it, to understand the aspirations of the Quebec people, of the French speaking people, and let me add they have here, in this house, a spendid opportunity to write history with us so that together we may become-and I say that in all seriousness- the fathers of the new confederation, the centenary of which will be celebrated in 1967.
We, French speaking Canadians, want to live side by side with our English speaking friends, but on an equal footing. We firmly believe that an economically strong Quebec will make Canada all the stronger.
If we want to have a strong unity, in this country, we must have strong components, and that is the objective that we in the province of Quebec are trying to reach at present.
For a long time, in the province of Quebec, we had difficulties to overcome in order to survive. This is why we had, for several years, an association called "La Survivance frangaise au Canada et en Amerique." That time is over. We have survived and we want now to live with you, according to our aspirations, but with you.
Do not be afraid if suddenly Quebec wants to live and wants its place under the sun. In Canada there is room for you and for us; we can work together to make this country of ours the finest in the world.
Mr. Speaker, as I told recently, in Toronto, our friends of the Toronto and district young Liberal association, what is happening now in Canada is somewhat like this story: a mother loved her baby but she loved him as a small baby and wanted him to remain small; her love for him was unequal but suddenly she saw him grow and became afraid. She did not know any longer what to make of her love in front of her growing baby.
I told them that something similar is happening here in Canada. Those who do not like it will have to pardon me, but in Quebec, it seems we are in the same situation as that little baby, neither too strong nor too weak, who was well loved, but now that he wants to grow up, not to take somebody's place, but to live side by side with his brothers, there are some people who seem to be frightened when they see him grow up.

The Address-Mr. Prud'homme
I tell you not to be frightened, not to listen to the voice of the extremists from any quarters. Personally, I firmly believe that the voice of reason will prevail over emotions, and the one who is speaking to you at this moment is a very emotional person indeed.
I think that as intelligent persons, we can build a great and prosperous Canada with the contribution of people who are not of English or French culture, and to them I say also: "Do not be afraid, but give us the benefit of your traditions, your culture, realizing that our country, Canada, is made up of two fundamental races and that together, we can surely hope for better days."
Mr. Speaker, we know that of all Canada's resources, the greatest and the most important is its double culture and its biracialism. Are we going to listen to those who, with a view to an electoral gain, in the hope of saving their seat or their party in this house, begin to use an extremist language? I say no.
Let us take for instance the kind of election campaign we have to face in our ridings. I wonder whether some of our leaders, whatever their political group, realize the full implications of their words? Let them stop spreading through the press and television a philosophy contrary to the general philosophy of our peaceful people.
They should think twice and try to find out from their listeners how they interpret their speeches. I say to those extremists from any part of our country that the young people give a different and violent interpretation to the words they uttered in so-called non-violent speeches.
I myself met in my riding, during the last election campaign, young extremists whom I unfortunately had to have arrested and whom my own friends went to bail for and whose fine they paid. But I had the painful obligation to have them arrested. Later on, they admitted that their appeals to a morbid nationalism had been misinterpreted.
I am certain, whatever the political party or the part of the country we belong to, that if we wish to sit down and work as intelligent people, we shall find a solution to the problem which confronts today, in 1964, our Canada, the centenary of which we are preparing to celebrate.
Why do we listen to the voice of extremists? Let us not forget that extremism begets extremism. Are we ready to drift towards one form of extremism or the other? I think not.
But, if such is the case, would it not be better for either of those ethnic groups in the country to find remedies applying to today's evils rather than wasting our energy to incite our population to sedition, than multiplying noisy press conferences, even

sponsored by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; would it not be better, I say, to find in the quiet of our offices a solution to unemployment and to the various ills presently in existence?

To my mind this is a terrible waste when they could be used in other countries of the world which really need them.
Having said that, I should like to discuss a matter which is of some general interest, and that is the question of a Canadian flag. Since the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) undertook to this house last year that Canada would have a distinctive flag within two years, and about a year of that time has now passed, I think a few remarks on this subject would be appropriate. However, I should like to make one thing clear, and that is that any remarks I may have to make on this subject in the next few moments are purely personal observations and do not purport to represent the viewpoint of the political party of which I am a member. As I say, these are purely personal observations.
Symbols of sovereignty such as a national flag are matters of deep emotional concern to most people. Not only are they matters of deep emotional concern but they are also matters of deep emotional conviction. Matters such as this and questions of moral importance-for example, capital punishment-are really matters which are suitable for a national referendum. However, I agree that it might be rather a difficult problem as far as a proposed national flag is concerned to have a referendum on that question, as there have been so many proposed designs submitted. Consequently, I think it is up to a member of parliament in such a case as this to be a delegate as far as his constituents are concerned, instead of a representative as defined by Mr. Burke in his well-known essay on the subject of parliament. In this case I think it is up to any hon. member to represent what appear and what he understands to be the views of his constituents on matters such as this-matters such as a national flag, or capital punishment, and so on.
If my mail is any indication in this matter, Mr. Speaker, the people in the constituency of Oxford seem to have a vast and overwhelming preference for the red ensign as the national flag of Canada. I have received a very large number of petitions and letters in this regard. I have had one or two suggestions to the contrary, but the overwhelming amount

of correspondence which I have received in this connection indicates a leaning toward this particular design.
I think it is very important, Mr. Speaker, to bring this matter to the attention of the house at this time. There has been a lot of discussion on this matter. Every hon. member of the house has had large quantities of mail suggesting different designs and a great number of members have made speeches in the house on this subject. And everyone is entitled to his own view on the matter. However, I think it should be made quite clear that there are a large number of people in this country who do prefer the red ensign as our national flag, and I wish to put that on record.
Now, Mr. Speaker, personally I am quite happy to accept and to support the red ensign as our national flag. However, I think it is only fair to note that it may be necessary at some time or other to make a compromise on the matter, and I have a few personal comments and suggestions on the essential elements of any national flag, and also on the proposed design, that I should like to submit for the consideration of this house and which might meet, if necessary and as an alternative, at least some of the many different points of view on this question.
Many views have been expressed, Mr. Speaker, on the subject of a national flag for Canada. Everyone knows, for instance, that the Canadian Legion, of which I am a member, is strongly in support of the red ensign. There are a very large number of other people in support of this design, too. On the other hand there have been many designs submitted of varying kinds. I think probably several thousand designs have been submitted over the years. Some of them are very interesting, some of them might be quite acceptable, and some are exceedingly bizarre. A competition was held recently by one of the newspapers in the country and most of the designs submitted to this paper were a conglomeration of multi-coloured squares triangles, circles, and various other abstract designs, which were so abstract and so subjective that I am sure they conveyed nothing to anyone except the author, and sometimes I doubt whether they even conveyed very much to the author. Therefore I do not think that most people in Canada would be very happy to accept a design of that character. I think it is also safe to say that there is no one group in Canada which is likely to be successful in that eventually in all likelihood some kind of compromise may well be necessary.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, a national flag -any national flag-should have three very distinctive characteristics about it. First of all, the flag should be distinctive, and I agree

with any hon. member in the house who has said in the past or will say in the future that the national flag of this country should be a distinctive one. Second, I think any such national flag should be reasonably simple of design. After all, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be facetious but young people do have to draw these things at school, and we do not want something which is practically impossible to draw: we want a nice flag of fairly simple design. Again, Mr. Speaker, a little more seriously, the third point I should like to make is that any national flag should not be something just dreamed up like some of these abstract designs to which I referred a few moments ago; a Canadian flag or any national flag should symbolize the institutions and the traditions of the country which it purports to represent. That, Mr. Speaker, is most important. We should not be ashamed of our background. We should not be ashamed of our institutions and traditions. They are here, and even if we do not like them we have to acknowledge them.
I should like to return once more to the red ensign, because that is a design which I have mentioned on several occasions. This is the choice of quite a number of people in Canada, as I have said. It is the choice of the Royal Canadian Legion, and in support of this choice they point out that the red ensign has accompanied Canadian forces into battle in two world wars and that a great many of our citizens of all racial backgrounds died beneath this flag in defence of the ideals which this country represents. In addition to that, the red ensign symbolizes much of our traditions and backgrounds. All that is quite true. There is also another point, and that is that many people in Canada wish the red ensign, regardless of the logic or reasoning of their argument. Many people in the country want the red ensign as our national flag. On the other hand, there are also a great many people in the country who do not wish the red ensign as our national flag.
One question which arises in my mind is this. Is the red ensign a distinctive flag? In some ways you could say it is, but outside of Canada it has been my experience, Mr. Speaker, that despite the coat of arms on the fly the red ensign of Canada is confused with the merchant marine flag of the British navy; to foreigners it looks very much like the old "red duster" of the British merchant marine; and in some cases it is even confused with the Bermudian flag. The design I would like to suggest for consideration of this house- and I am not suggesting this design is going to receive wide acclaim, although I would hope people would give it consideration at some future time-is that instead of the red
The Address-Mr. Nesbitt ensign we substitute a white ensign, and instead of the Canadian coat of arms on the fly we have a large green maple leaf surrounded by three royal blue fleurs de lis, with a gold band at the bottom. You say: Why would you suggest that? It is very simple. First of all I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, it is a simple design; actually if you had to draw these things, it would be quite simple.
Why does one suggest these particular things? Well, in my opinion as I have already mentioned the symbols on a national flag must represent the background of history and institutions of our country, and I say our country has a background of which none of us has any reason to be ashamed whatsoever. The union jack symbolizes certainly many of the traditions we have inherited from Great Britain, such as parliamentary government, our system of justice, freedom of speech and many other things.
The white background, rather than the red one, is one of the original colours of French speaking Canada, and the three royal blue fleur-de-lis, and the gold band are also symbols of the French culture that has contributed so very, very much to this country.
The maple leaf is a symbol of something that is purely Canadian. I know some of our American friends might say there are maple trees in the United States too, but I know in most parts of the world the maple leaf is associated with Canada.

Speaking of tricks, Mr. Speaker, it really was a trick.
First of all, in the field of agriculture: I remember when, during last session, I made a speech to commend the government in power for having at last, included some legislation to create a department for eastern agriculture in the speech from the throne. I can assure you that my enthusiasm has been much dampened during that session, because I saw our chances of at last obtaining the hoped for department becoming more and more remote.

This year, you may be assured that the farmers in my riding are most disagreeably surprised to see one of their greatest hopes vanishing in this way.
Mr. Speaker, I am told that another organization may perhaps replace that department, but I wonder whether it will be able to answer all the needs of the province of Quebec. I shall just say that I consider it very doubtful. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), is well aware of it, because, first of all, agriculture is under provincial jurisdiction and second, because the western provinces would lose a few cents, which would be most prejudicial in a future election.
Then, what are we doing? We are playing on words, we draw back, we go forward, we hesitate; it is precisely, on the other hand, one of the characteristics of the present government: indecision.
This should prove to you, Mr. Speaker, how much risk you run when you trespass on other people's property. Nevertheless, the Liberal government takes mischievous pleasure in making such incursions in the province of Quebec, sometimes in the field of agriculture, some other times in the field of education or health insurance. And as a maniac who proves repentant, it constantly falls again into the same errors. In fact, during each election, the Liberals swear to amend, to do better in the future; they promise before the people to leave Quebec alone, but the day after, they cannot help it, old habits come back and their perverse feelings awake. Therefore, reading each speech from the throne, the opposition parties are all amazed at the new pranks of the Liberals in the field of provincial property. At first, they seemed repentant, since they promised not to do it again, but today, they have become dangerous, even sadistic, for they advise us they will continue to plunder the province of Quebec, but that, in future, once the heinous crime is committed, they will inform the beautiful province.
And I see all our nice little French Canadians, in their seats behind their leader, happy at this invasion of Quebec's territory.
There is an invasion of the economic field, the educational field, the social field and even of the territory itself, since one third of our territory on the coast of Labrador is slipping away from us.
Our little Liberal friends secure in the warm comfort of the small victory which their slush funds gave them at the polls are sleeping peacefully until a new election comes along.
To them, it is the party that has to be saved, even if it means the death of a nation.

But can you not see, gentlemen, that this is precisely the kind of partisanship that has weakened Canada?
After such a betrayal of your mandate, by not intervening to stop your leaders, even at your private caucuses, how will you dare face again your fellow citizens?
No, the dialogue must begin before it is too late.
And that dialogue must first begin at Liberal caucuses level to reach all parties. In order to discuss, we must take the time to sit down and centre our thoughts on a given point. That is to say, all people concerned must stop once and for all dancing ceaselessly first on one foot then on the other, as boxers do.
Indeed, the government claims in all newspapers, that it will end those famous joint programs and then in the speech from the throne it comes up with new ones. There is something wrong somewhere, and we are not to blame; indeed, we are going from surprise to surprise with regard to a government which is certainly not sure of itself.
Are we going to watch unperturbed that premeditated infringement by Ottawa upon Quebec's prerogatives?
Infringement upon fields that are the most sacred for the provinces and that the 1867 confederation act was to guarantee.
And then they have the nerve to say: what have you got to complain about?
Keep quiet, let us dispossess you and do not resist.
And as a tranquilizer, a new drug has been invented: co-operative federalism. What a joke.
The most centralizing party the country has ever known is now talking about cooperation. And to top it all, right when it wants to put this federal-provincial co-operation at work, it loses no time undermining the last possessions.
I think that the present government has made a fool of itself long enough and that it is time for the provinces, at least the province of Quebec, to assert themselves.
And I hope with all my heart that there will arise in Quebec a leader strong enough to save what is left of the rights of the French Canadians.
We have to bow to facts. If the provinces have created this monster, the federal government, it is their responsibility to limit the, damage it can cause.
I feel that the only solution would be for Quebec to get back its own rights in the field of agriculture and for the federal government to give up a very unbecoming responsibility.
I wish to mention another oversight in the speech from the throne. It is about family allowances. Last year we were told once 20220-29
The Address-Mr. Gauthier more that they would be increased, but there is not a single word about it in the speech from the throne.
"I remember". When I say those words, Mr. Speaker, I think of the interesting speech the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) made the other day when he described so nicely the heroism of French Canadians who lost their lives for their country, and I would like the hon. member for Leeds to take note -I say that the motto of the province of Quebec "Je me souviens" much transcends the limits of Dieppe.
We remember that our forefathers came to Canada armed with faith and equipped with a plough. We remember also that another people came later, armed with the sword. Moreover, we remember that during the American aggression of 1812, the British appealed to the French Canadians, and that the two great nations which constituted our country at the time, joined together to defend Canada. The British people asked the French Canadians for help. The latter have answered: yes, we shall defend Canada but on one condition, on the condition that our rights will be safeguarded in the future.
Out of this, our constitution was born. You have there, Mr. Speaker, the constitution for the whole of Canada.
That constitution we remember well and it is for it that we are pleading today so that our rights guaranteed by this constitution, will not be jeopardized.
Mr. Speaker, I have something else to say. I shall be brief, for I have been allowed ten minutes only. I should like to speak about two other points that are most important to our country. I am referring to the Canada Elections Act, and especially to the section that governs votation.
As I had always taken part in elections in rural areas, I was wondering what the procedure was like in large towns, like Montreal, to have men elected who had been defeated two or three times before, in other towns.
I have had the answer to this query during the last by-election of February 10, 1964.
I spent three days in Montreal, including voting day, in order to find out how the old parties' electoral machine works.
I found out, first of all, that anyone could vote, and as many times as they could collect forms left by the enumerator to each resident of the electoral district.
Since only 20 per cent of the voters go the polls, you will understand how easy it is for one who wants to vote in all the polls to secure the necessary certificates by changing his name in each voting poll.
That is why I said a moment ago that a mere 20 per cent of the Montreal voters go

The Address-Mr. Gauthier to the polls. Probably halt of the votes are cast by people who like to vote more than once.
Mr. Speaker, I hear voices on the other side, while I am discussing which party is more ailing. I am getting to see which one it is.
To give you an idea of the problem, let us say that a party decides to pass off 20 to 25 irregular ballots per poll-which are commonly called "telegraphes" in French. When the polls close at seven o'clock at night you will see the same thing as happened in Montreal during the last election when there was a majority of 6,200 for 310 polls.
I could not positively state that this accounts for the last majorities, but the validity of our elections should be seriously questioned.
And what is more serious, Mr. Speaker, is that neither of the old-line parties want to change radically the Canada Elections Act.
Why are they against any reform? Is it because both play the same game? It might be precisely that race to the poll in order to cast the greatest possible number of votes by the fewer people possible that has been called an electoral contest.
I am under the impression that if another party managed to defeat this instrument of finance and succeeded in coming into power, it would discover some pretty things following an investigation on the election methods of old line parties.
I am therefore challenging the two old-line parties to amend the Canada Elections Act and to make compulsory the identification card with picture and fingerprints.
Election lists should be permanent and the administration of oath on voting day should be abolished.
Such reforms alone would be a proof a sincerity on the part of the old line parties. The refusal to introduce them would be proof of their guilt.
However, I am convinced that nothing will be done, because the only wish of old-line parties is to cause confusion, confusion among elected members and confusion among electors.
Where are we going, what are we? Are we British subjects in a Canadian country or Canadians in a British country?
That is the question facing many young people and also older ones who have not been submitted yet to the dictatorship of the old parties under which the French speaking element supplies the co-operation while the English speaking element supplies the factor No. 1 of centralizing federalism to which the Liberals have now given a new name, that

is co-operative federalism, no doubt to hide the old solution. But the result will always be the same.
And while this operation goes on, what do we see on the political screen? A prime minister shouting to the four winds in a desperate effort to soothe the French speaking patient who asks nothing more than to live under the 1867 constitution.
The Prime Minister looks strangely like the anaesthetist who administers the drugs according to the patient's resistance.
We hear demands concerning provincial autonomy, respect of provincial rights by the central government and the return of taxation powers to the provinces, so that they may again be independent states within a free country in accordance with the spirit of confederation.
In fact, we realize that today we do not have independent states nor a free country because in politics we are nothing but British colonials, whereas our economy is 80 per cent in the hands of the United States. The provinces are the powerless victims of the capitalist and centralizing government in Ottawa. Under such circumstances, how can there be a dialogue? We are a country without a leader and without possessions.
Indeed, if England demanded her royalty rights and if the United States claimed their economic dues, what would be left to us? Nothing. In that respect, India is far ahead of us. And who we are discussing? What for? I think it would be very difficult, even for government members, to give me a clear answer. And the hypocrisy which prevails in this house proves my point.
Let us start at the beginning, that is let us agree on the principle of a country, of Canada. What are we, from Quebec, asking for? We are asking for one thing. We do not want to take any other essential rights away from Ottawa, but we firmly object to Ottawa taking any more of our essential rights. We are asking Ottawa to stop the frantic invasion of the rights of Quebec so that we can, if necessary, give a new definition of the rights and responsibilities on both sides.
We want Ottawa to give a chance to the French Canadians to develop their province at the same rate as the others, in order to make our contribution to the building of our great country, Canada.
We want this jungle law, which always gives Ottawa the lion's share, to be abolished once and for all. We want the great French Canadian nation to walk proudly beside the Anglo-Saxon nation, equally great. It is in that perspective that we see Canada's future.

It is also the only way that will lead to understanding between the two nations which confederation was intended to make equal partners.
I trust that in placing the discussion in that light, all Canadians of goodwill will surely come to an understanding wholeheartedly desired by all Canadians, whether they be French or English speaking.
We believe that the time for idle talk is over, and that after 97 years, we should strive towards a great, united and strong Canada.

speechtext:
I, too, should like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address-the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Cote) and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford).
I wish to take a few minutes of the time of the house to talk about the Canada pension plan. During the debate on the speech from the throne many members of the official opposition have referred to this plan, sometimes obliquely, often with disparaging comments. One hon. member devoted his whole speech to an attack on many features of the plan which is to be submitted to this parliament for its approval. I refer to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken). After reading his speech in Hansard it would seem to me that, in summary, it falls under these several headings. First, he says the plan does not cover a sufficient number of our people; he complains it is not wide enough laterally. Second, he says that those Canadian citizens who are covered are not covered adequately. In the third place, he tells us this Canada pension plan would have inflationary effects. Another point he makes is that because it is partially funded it would constitute a drain on our investment resources. That contention is, I think, somewhat contradictory of his previous statement. It also seems to me that his statement about inflation is somewhat inconsistent with the two points he made about inadequacy of coverage.
Then the hon. member went on to say that the rate of contribution of 2 per cent-1 per cent from employees and 1 per cent from employers-was insufficient to maintain a fund of this kind. He pointed out that under private schemes the rate was 4 per cent to 6 per cent, and that this 2 per cent basis could not possibly work. Again, I suggest that this is somewhat contradictory of his previous contention that even at 2 per cent the fund would be a considerable drain on the investment resources of the country. The hon. member went on to indicate that it was impossible for the private plans to co-ordinate with our
The Address-Mr. Munro plan because the average Canadian under the Canadian pension plan could not predetermine at the time of the commencement of his contribution what his pension at retirement would be.
I think, now, I have given the house a fair summary of the points which have been brought up in criticism of the plan not only by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka but by many others. I think it can be stated that not only do many of these points contradict each other but they are certainly inconsistent with the facts of this plan as they have been revealed to the house. I point out also, that in the conclusion of his attack on the various features of the plan the hon. member said he was opposed-I do not know whether he was speaking for his party -to a parliamentary committee being constituted to, as he put it, ram this plan through the house. Well, this is the first time in my experience I have ever heard the setting up of a parliamentary committee being interpreted as a device to ram something through the house. If an argument of that type has validity it must give any government pause when considering the advisability of constituting parliamentary committees in future to discuss such issues as these. As a matter of fact, I think it is only fair to say that the setting up of a parliamentary committee should be interpreted in some other light, rather than suggesting it is a means of trying to ram something through the house. In fact, of course, it will give a valuable opportunity for members of the house to discuss many of the features of the proposal.
In any event, these are the grounds upon which this plan has been attacked not only by members of the opposition but by the premier of Ontario. These attacks have one thing in common, it seems to me. In all of them, whatever their length or scope, there does not seem to be any indication either from the hon. member to whom I have referred or from any other member of the official opposition, or from one premier, as to just what kind of plan would be preferred. They are not advising this house or the Canadian people of any reasonable alternative. They content themselves with a summary indictment along the lines I have indicated.
However, a most serious piece of misinformation was brought into this house by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka when he stated that 81 per cent of the Canadian people would not be covered by this plan.
I think this is how he got the final figure up to over 14 million people. First of all, he included five and a half million people from Quebec. Of course, they are not counted in this contributory Canada pension scheme,

The Address-Mr. Munro because it has been indicated they are going ahead with a contributory scheme of their own. Surely, the hon. member would not suggest that we should cover Canadian citizens in Quebec who do not even contribute to the plan. The hon. member then included over 700,000 old age pensioners presently over 70. Apparently the fact that this is a contributory plan based on wage earnings completely escapes him. These old age pensioners were covered by legislative action taken in this house when we voted a $10 increase in old age security benefits. If the hon. member, or any other hon. member of this house, feels that something additional should be done for them, surely it is not suggested that coverage should be given under a contributory scheme when these people are retired, and not earning wages, and when it is openly acknowledged that the present plan is based on contributions from wage earners. Surely the hon. member is clouding the issue when he talks about 714,000 people over 70 not included in the plan. If he is disturbed about the level of benefits to these people then, surely, he should talk about amending the Old Age Security Act for he is certainly not talking about the Canada pension plan.
The hon. member then went on to talk about children and widows. For some reason he did not attach a numerical figure to this. He then talked about the sick and the disabled, the unemployed, single women at home, the self-employed with small wages, and casual labourers. To suggest that these people are not covered by the plan is just ludicrous. Can we seriously suggest that under the Canada pension plan a single woman is never at any time, from the time she is 18 to the time she retires at 65 or 70, going to be in a position to contribute to the scheme either on a voluntary basis or as an employee? So when an attempt is made to count every female person over the age of 18 and include her in a figure of 14 million, we soon see how ridiculous these figures are-how ludicrous they are.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: Right there I think we can recover a goodly number of the three million people who are in this grand total of 14 million, to say nothing of the 714,000 people over age 70 who should never have been included in the first place. Then the hon. member arrived at a grand total of six million in this over-all figure under the age of 18 who would receive, in his words, little benefit under the plan. I am now referring to Canadians under the age of 18. On the face of it this also is ridiculous. These six million people will also have to be deducted from the grand total of 14 million, for the simple reason that they, as far as I am aware, are not complaining about being included in a Canada pension scheme. They represent a goodly portion of the 70 per cent of the Canadian people who are covered by no pension scheme at all. These are the people in many of our ridings who are most vociferous in wanting the implementation of a Canada pension plan. These are many of the people who want to be helped in their desire to take care of their parents, who wish some alleviation of the hardship and onus of worrying about the support of their parents when they attain old age. So they are more than happy to have the implementation of a Canada pension scheme on a contributory basis to which their parents can now contribute and obtain full benefit at the end of a maturity period of ten years. Certainly if the hon. member is talking about persons of 18 years and under in his riding, he has a most peculiar riding, because I have not noticed any similar sentiments anywhere that I have been.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: Perhaps I may continue, Mr. Speaker. These six million people will be participating in the plan; they will themselves obtain benefit on retirement. These six million people will have parents who will receive benefit under the Canada pension plan. Therefore perhaps it is not too outlandish for us to deduct these approximately six million people from the grand total of 14 million.

The hon. member went on to arrive at his grand total of 14 million by talking about part-time employees and seasonal employees. Again, he did not put a number on these. When you put back the

six million Canadians under the age of 18 and the three million people, many of whom are made up of single women over 18 to age 65, you see that we have gone a long way to recovering the great percentage of Canadian citizens who are going to benefit from the implementation of this plan.
There are one or two other points I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, and which I think should be emphasized in defence of the Canada pension scheme. After all, I think we must all concede that this plan will be of great significance to the Canadian people. I can think of no other national issue that is more important. I can think of no other national issue that will benefit more many of our urban areas and many of the agricultural areas, especially farmers who have not sufficient means to take care of themselves adequately in their old age.
These people are most concerned about the implementation of this plan. Surely it is something that should be considered seriously. Certainly it is something that should not be subject to rampant misinformation deluged upon this house. Certainly it is something to which we should give every type of consideration. I am not saying for a moment that we should not have honest discussion on it. I am not saying there should not be criticism of it. But it should be constructive criticism. To just go through a list of points as ludicrous as those which have been put forward and try to build them into an argument against the Canada pension plan seems to me anything but constructive. At the conclusion of a ludicrous argument such as was put forward, no reasonable alternative at all was presented for consideration by this house.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext:
The hon. member talked-I think this should be on the record-about the wives and children of breadwinners who would not be covered because there was no survivorship or dependency of benefits. I would point out that the hon. member says a man could pay into the Canada pension plan for 40 years-I think these were his words- and at age 64 neither he, his wife nor his children would receive any benefit from the plan. He is wrong when he says that. I think this can be pointed out by all the literature that has already been distributed on the plan,
The Address-Mr. Munro and these are the facts. If a contributor such as the hon. member spoke of dies at the age of 65, his widow will be able to receive at age 65 a pension of 60 per cent of the benefit he would have received. If he is over age 65 at the date of death and is receiving benefit, she will be entitled to receive 60 per cent of his benefit, provided she is over age 65. Thus there are benefits for survivors under the Canada pension plan.
What about married contributors at age 65 or over who will receive no earnings-related pension for their wives? In this case, if the wife of such a contributor is 65 or over she will be entitled to an old age security pension. Therefore a man and wife both aged 65 or over will receive more in benefits than will a single person of the same age. Surely these facts, which are on record, completely debunk any suggestion that there is no survivor benefit under this plan.
Another point which was raised by the hon. member and repeated by others was the question of the unemployed and disabled. I think one fact that has been missed in this whole argument is the average 10 per cent dropout provision. As hon. members know from reading the literature, the Canada pension plan actually takes into account the fact that there will be some people who will be unemployed or disabled part of their lives. This is true. As has been stated in the material already released in regard to the Canada pension plan, there will be excluded from the calculation of a person's average earnings, his earnings in 10 per cent of the years from the end of the transitional period-the first 10-year maturity period-to the date of his retirement. This provision is to ensure that when a person's earnings in some years are abnormally low, or zero, because of sickness or unemployment or for other reasons such as disability, those earnings will be excluded from the calculation. Such a person will not, therefore, be excessively penalized. Surely this gives considerable leeway to those people who suffer sickness, unemployment or disability of some kind. I think this point has been missed completely in the arguments which have been advanced to date.
I wish to point out one other thing. After this attack on some of the features of the plan, especially with reference to those who allegedly would not be covered, the hon. member went on to say that this pension scheme would create a great drain on the investment resources of the country. Presumably he is talking about private investment, and presumably he feels that if there is any public investment in this country or any additional funds put at public disposal through government agencies, this is not

The Address-Mr. Munro going to lend itself to the development of the country, but only when it is in private hands. That is a traditional concept that he has every right to espouse; but I am afraid he will find many in this house who will not agree with him. However, this is his argument. He went on to say, after making this point, that he felt there should be a more generous allotment among the provinces. Surely he is contradicting himself there. If he feels that this will cause a drain on resources if the scheme is funded in this way, it will also create the same drain on our resources no matter whether the funds are placed at the disposal of the federal government or at the disposal of the provinces, or by whatever means the investment is made. So there seems to be considerable inconsistency in that argument.
Then the hon. member goes on to ask where the money will come from. He talks in his speech about 2 per cent being completely inadequate and that it will take a long time to build up the fund. Then he says, as reported on page 323 of Hansard:
It cannot be sound on payments of 2 per cent on a person's income because private trusts and insurance companies, and even Canadian government annuities, can only be found sound on the basis of something between 4 per cent and 6 per cent of income.
I would point out here that a good portion of the over-all total, namely, the wage related contributory part of the pension comes, it is true, from contributions, but at least half, $75 comes out of the old age security fund, which is not composed of contributions at all. This point must have been forgotten when the hon. member suggested that the 2 per cent is not sound. He arrived at his figures by comparing the rates of private plans, where the whole amount is financed by the contributors.
I think the hon. member has also forgotten another point when he compares the plan with private plans. He has forgotten that under this scheme the wage related contributory part of the old age security payment is regarded as a minimum contribution with minimum benefits. The old age pension is for people to live on. When the hon. member talks about more than 6 per cent being required he must be talking, and in many cases is talking, about pension plans which

provide far more excessive benefits than will be provided under this plan. These benefits must be regarded as a minimum. So on these two points alone he cannot be regarded as serious when he advances the suggestion that the plan is unsound, and uses as a comparison rates required by private companies with plans not similar in any degree to this one, and which do not take into account the old age security feature as does the plan which we are bringing forward to parliament.
